title: Stem torsion on rough supports is a mechanical couple from adhesion, not an adaptation

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Stem torsion on rough supports is a mechanical couple from adhesion, not an adaptation

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Twining stems become twisted on rough supports but not on smooth ones because adhesion to the rough support sets up a mechanical couple, so Darwin's adaptive explanation (gaining rigidity) is unnecessary.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In the case of the roughened support, there is a temporary adhesion or “clinging” between it and the growing stem which twines around it; and a system of forces is thus set up, producing a “couple,” just as it was in the case of the ram’s or antelope’s horn through direct adhesion of the bony core to the surrounding sheath.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Torsion in climbing plants”. Scope: twining stems of climbing plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-11: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.49

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The proposed mechanical couple yields a clean controlled test. Public observational plant records do not contain the force, adhesion and torsion measurements needed to distinguish it from adaptive or developmental alternatives.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare genetically and developmentally matched stems twining on supports differing only in calibrated roughness, measuring adhesion, torque and stem torsion over time. Torsion scaling with adhesion-generated torque supports the claim; equal torsion on smooth supports or no torque-torsion link refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Support roughness also changes contact geometry and plant behavior.

The required controlled rough-versus-smooth time series is not known as a reusable public dataset.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The contrast between rough and smooth supports is a clear experimental criterion and would separate a frictional couple from a general gain in rigidity. That experiment is not available as a reusable public dataset, and published accounts do not include the sample sizes and twist angles needed for a modern reanalysis. Resolving the claim requires new measurements or recovery of data that have not been deposited.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Grow matched twining stems on rough and smooth supports and measure torsion of the stem, adhesion, and bending stiffness. A mechanical couple is supported if twist appears with measured clinging on rough supports and disappears on smooth ones of equal diameter; an adaptive-rigidity account would require a stiffness benefit even where adhesion is absent.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Darwin's smooth-versus-rough comparison is a narrative experiment, not an archived measurement table.

No current public dataset records stem torsion, support roughness, and rigidity together.
